item.content:encoded:
Crestview High School's band program has earned a prestigious national honor, becoming the first Florida band to receive the Earl D. Irons Program of Distinction Award, according to WKRG News 5.

The distinction recognizes excellence in music education and represents rare recognition for a high school band program. The award places Crestview among the nation's top-tier music programs and highlights the quality of instruction and student achievement within the band.

This achievement comes as part of ongoing efforts by the Santa Rosa County school district to strengthen its arts and music programs. The award reflects years of dedication from the band's directors and the commitment of students who participated in rehearsals, performances, and competitions leading up to the honor.

item.title: Georgia Teacher Creates 'Fart Corner' For Students
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: A second-grade teacher in Georgia has gone viral for creating an unconventional classroom space designed to help students manage a very natural bodily function. According to Today.com, teacher Candy Sydney-Browning established what she calls a "gas station" in her classroom—essentially a designated area where students can step away if they need to…
item.content:encoded:
A second-grade teacher in Georgia has gone viral for creating an unconventional classroom space designed to help students manage a very natural bodily function. According to Today.com, teacher Candy Sydney-Browning established what she calls a "gas station" in her classroom—essentially a designated area where students can step away if they need to pass gas without disrupting the learning environment.

The creative approach to classroom management has drawn attention for addressing a real issue that teachers face: kids being embarrassed or disruptive when they need to relieve themselves of intestinal gas. By creating a low-pressure zone where students can step out of the main classroom temporarily, Sydney-Browning aims to reduce classroom interruptions and help students feel less self-conscious.

While the concept might seem unusual, educators have praised the teacher's innovative thinking about creating a comfortable learning space where students can address basic bodily needs without shame or distraction.

item.title: Two Decades Later, 9/11 Justice Still Waits at Guantanamo
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: More than 20 years after the September 11th terrorist attacks, the legal process against key defendants remains stalled at Guantanamo Bay, according to reporting from ABC News Senior Investigative Reporter Aaron Katersky. Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and four co-defendants have appeared before military tribunals, but the proceedings have moved at a…
item.content:encoded:
More than 20 years after the September 11th terrorist attacks, the legal process against key defendants remains stalled at Guantanamo Bay, according to reporting from ABC News Senior Investigative Reporter Aaron Katersky.

Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and four co-defendants have appeared before military tribunals, but the proceedings have moved at a glacial pace. Katersky's reporting, highlighted in InWeekly's latest edition, suggests the government's efforts to bring the alleged architects of the attacks to justice have fallen short of the swift accountability promised to grieving families and a nation still processing the tragedy.

The delays raise questions about the legal and procedural complexities surrounding military commissions, as well as broader debates over detention and prosecution at the controversial naval base prison. Families of 9/11 victims have long expressed frustration with the pace of prosecutions, with some cases taking nearly as long as the wars themselves have lasted.

item.title: Escambia County Turns Off License Plate Readers After Year-Long Privacy Fight
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Automated license plate readers that have monitored traffic across Escambia County are now offline following nearly a year of local debate over privacy and government surveillance. The ALPR cameras, which scan and record vehicle license plates, became a flashpoint for residents and officials worried about Fourth Amendment protections and data…
item.content:encoded:
Automated license plate readers that have monitored traffic across Escambia County are now offline following nearly a year of local debate over privacy and government surveillance.

The ALPR cameras, which scan and record vehicle license plates, became a flashpoint for residents and officials worried about Fourth Amendment protections and data collection by authorities. The technology had supporters who argued it helps law enforcement track stolen vehicles and wanted suspects, but critics questioned whether the surveillance was worth the privacy trade-offs.

According to InWeekly, the issue united an unusual coalition of residents across the political spectrum—from civil liberties advocates to conservatives concerned about government overreach—all questioning how the county should handle the camera systems and what happened to the data they collected.

The decision to deactivate the readers marks the end of a contentious local debate that reflected broader national concerns about surveillance technology and its place in communities. It remains unclear whether the county will pursue alternative public safety technologies or revisit the ALPR program in the future.

item.title: Pensacola Launches Civic Dialogues Platform to Crowdsource Community Ideas
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: The City of Pensacola has rolled out a new online initiative called Civic Dialogues, partnering with change.org to gather and prioritize resident input on local issues. Running through October 12th, the platform invites any Pensacola resident to submit ideas, vote on neighbors' suggestions, and help shape the community's priorities. The project…
item.content:encoded:
The City of Pensacola has rolled out a new online initiative called Civic Dialogues, partnering with change.org to gather and prioritize resident input on local issues. Running through October 12th, the platform invites any Pensacola resident to submit ideas, vote on neighbors' suggestions, and help shape the community's priorities. The project launched September 3rd and is accessible at civicdialogues.org/pensacola.

The platform is designed to give residents a structured way to weigh in on what matters most to the city. Rather than relying on traditional town halls or comment periods, Civic Dialogues lets ideas bubble up organically and shows which concepts have the strongest community support.

Residents interested in participating have just over a month to post suggestions, comment on existing ideas, or simply vote on proposals from other community members. The city hasn't specified how the feedback will influence policy decisions, but the initiative represents an effort to directly engage residents in civic planning.

item.content:encoded:
Festival season is ramping up across the Pensacola area, and organizers are putting the final touches on events that have been in the works for months. The 49th Annual Pensacola Seafood Festival is among the major draws coming this fall, according to the Fiesta Pensacola Foundation.

"We have been gearing up for this for months," said Fiesta Pensacola Foundation Director Margaret-Anne West. The festival is one of several major community events scheduled as the weather cools and outdoor gatherings become more popular in Northwest Florida.

Fall festivals typically draw thousands of visitors to the Pensacola area and feature local food, music, crafts, and family entertainment. The seafood festival, in particular, showcases regional restaurants and vendors highlighting fresh catches from the Gulf of Mexico.

item.content:encoded:
A major traveling exhibition from the Smithsonian Institution is heading to Atmore this month. According to the Poarch Creek Indians, the "Americans" exhibit will be on display at the Strand Theater starting September 16th and running through November.

The exhibition explores the diverse stories and experiences that have shaped American identity and culture. It's part of the Smithsonian's broader effort to bring curated collections and interactive displays to communities across the country.

The Strand Theater in Atmore will serve as the venue for the monthlong showcase. Residents in the region looking for cultural programming and educational exhibits will have the opportunity to explore the installation during its run in Escambia County's neighboring area.

item.title: Uthmeier Pushes For Criminal Penalties On AI Companies
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier says he'll push new legislation imposing criminal penalties on tech companies whose A-I chatbots aid or abet crimes. The proposal would target companies with control over an A-I product's design and safety settings, allowing for fines, victim payments, and even suspension of…
item.content:encoded: Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier says he'll push new legislation imposing criminal penalties on tech companies whose A-I chatbots aid or abet crimes. The proposal would target companies with control over an A-I product's design and safety settings, allowing for fines, victim payments, and even suspension of activity in the state. It follows Uthmeier's ongoing investigation into ChatGPT's use by the alleged F-S-U shooter. Uthmeier says legislation likely won't move until the next regular session in March.

item.title: EPA funding green-lights Bay Minette environmental assessment
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Bay Minette officials are moving ahead with environmental cleanup efforts at the former Standard Furniture building site, thanks to a new round of EPA funding. The South Alabama Regional Planning Commission has received the grant to conduct a comprehensive assessment of the property, according to city leaders. The assessment is a key first step in…
item.content:encoded:
Bay Minette officials are moving ahead with environmental cleanup efforts at the former Standard Furniture building site, thanks to a new round of EPA funding. The South Alabama Regional Planning Commission has received the grant to conduct a comprehensive assessment of the property, according to city leaders.

The assessment is a key first step in preparing the long-vacant industrial site for potential redevelopment. Bay Minette has been seeking to breathe new life into the aging facility, which has sat underutilized for years and represents both a blight concern and an opportunity for economic revival in the Baldwin County city.

The EPA funding underscores growing regional interest in brownfield reclamation projects across the eastern Gulf Coast. Similar environmental assessments have become critical tools for communities looking to transform former industrial properties into mixed-use developments, commercial space, or other productive uses. Officials say the evaluation will clarify what remediation steps, if any, may be needed before the property can move forward.
